scenes.narration: DynamoDB scales horizontally by physically splitting a table across partitions, and which partition any single item lands on is decided entirely by one attribute you choose at design time: the partition key. Choose it well and the table genuinely does look infinitely scalable. Choose it badly and you can get throttled while the table's overall capacity sits nowhere near exhausted. This chapter maps to Design High-Performing Architectures, twenty four percent of the associate exam, and Design Resilient Architectures, twenty six percent, and it's built around exactly one sentence: the partition key is a physical placement decision, not just a logical identifier.

facts.label: The one decision that matters
facts.value: The partition key is hashed to decide physical placement — not just a logical label

facts.label: The hard, stable ceiling
facts.value: Maximum item size: 400 KB, regardless of key design or capacity mode

scenes.narration: Here's the plausible-sounding mistake. DynamoDB is famous for scaling to enormous size without capacity planning, so it's tempting to assume any attribute that's roughly present on every item — a status flag, a country code — is a perfectly fine partition key, because DynamoDB will supposedly spread the load around no matter what you pick. It's an understandable mistake, because DynamoDB's aggregate scale really is virtually unlimited. But aggregate table capacity and per-item access patterns are two completely different things, and a table can have enormous total capacity while still throttling badly if a lot of requests target the same handful of key values.

props.heading: "DynamoDB scales automatically, so the key barely matters"
bullets: A status flag, a country code, a signup date — anything present on most items feels like a safe partition key.
A huge aggregate capacity number feels like proof that no single value can ever get overloaded.
"It's NoSQL" quietly turns into "key mistakes can be patched later," the way you'd add an index to a relational table.

scenes.narration: Here's the actual mechanism. DynamoDB hashes the partition key value to determine which physical partition an item lives on, and every item sharing that same value lands in the same item collection, on the same partition, sharing that one partition's slice of throughput. Low cardinality concentrates traffic by construction — a handful of distinct values means a handful of overloaded partitions, no matter how large the table's total capacity is. DynamoDB's adaptive capacity feature does automatically shift more throughput toward busy partitions, and it genuinely helps, but it's a secondary safety net, not a substitute for a good key. The tell on exam day: throttling correlated with one specific attribute value, while the table's overall capacity is nowhere near used up.

props.heading: Hashing decides where an item physically lives
bullets: Every item sharing a partition key value lands in the same item collection, on the same physical partition.
Low cardinality concentrates traffic by construction — no amount of aggregate capacity fixes an overloaded single value.
Adaptive capacity shifts throughput toward hot partitions automatically, but it's a mitigation, not a design substitute.
The tell: throttling tied to one attribute value while overall table capacity sits far from exhausted.

scenes.narration: Picture the same stream of requests run against three different key designs. A key built on a status field with only three possible values piles almost everything onto two or three partitions out of many, and it starts throttling fast, even with plenty of spare capacity elsewhere. Add a random suffix to that same status value and the load spreads wider, softening the hot spot without eliminating the underlying shape. Switch to something genuinely high-cardinality, like a user ID, and the exact same request volume spreads evenly across every partition with zero throttling — which is what horizontal scaling actually looks like underneath, and it's a direct consequence of the key, not something DynamoDB does for you regardless of choice.

props.heading: Same request stream, three partition key designs

rows.label: status (3 values)
cells: Piles onto 2-3 partitions out of many
Throttles fast, even with spare capacity elsewhere

rows.label: status + random suffix
cells: Spread wider, hot spot softened
Fewer throttles — sharding helps without fixing the root shape

rows.label: UserId (high cardinality)
cells: Even across every partition
Zero throttling — this is real horizontal scale

scenes.narration: Four mechanisms this chapter leans on constantly, and the exam loves testing whether you keep them straight. A Global Secondary Index — G S I — gets its own partition key, letting you query the same data by something completely different, and it can be bolted on any time, but its reads are always eventually consistent, never strong. A Local Secondary Index — L S I — keeps the base table's exact partition key and only changes the sort order, which does support strongly consistent reads, but it has to be defined the moment the table is created and can never be added afterward. DynamoDB Accelerator, DAX for short, is a pure read-side cache that gets hot items down to microsecond latency without touching key design at all — it does nothing for a write-side hot partition. And adaptive capacity just runs in the background, automatically, shifting throughput toward whichever partitions are busiest right now.

props.heading: GSI vs LSI vs DAX vs adaptive capacity

rows.label: Global Secondary Index
cells: Own partition key — query the same data a different way
Yes, any time — but always eventually consistent

rows.label: Local Secondary Index
cells: Same partition key, different sort key
No — table-creation only, but supports strong consistency

rows.label: DAX
cells: In-memory cache for hot reads, microsecond latency
Yes, purely additive — has zero effect on writes

rows.label: Adaptive capacity
cells: Auto-shifts throughput toward busy partitions
Always on — a safety net, not a key-design fix

scenes.narration: Boil the whole chapter down and almost every scenario question sorts into one of five buckets: where does an item physically live, that's the partition key; how is it ordered where it lives, that's the sort key; is there a genuinely different way to query it, that's a G S I or an L S I; how fast does a hot read need to be, that's DAX; and how is capacity paid for, provisioned for steady traffic you can plan, or on-demand for traffic you can't. Reach for a better key whenever throttling is tied to specific values with capacity to spare — more capacity never fixes that on its own.

props.heading: Five buckets cover nearly every DynamoDB question

rows.label: Global Secondary Index
cells: Query by a different attribute, maybe added after the table already exists

rows.label: Local Secondary Index
cells: A different sort order over the same partition key, decided at table creation

rows.label: DAX
cells: The bottleneck is repeated reads of the same hot items

rows.label: Better partition key design
cells: Requests throttle on a subset of key values despite spare aggregate capacity

rows.label: On-demand capacity
cells: Traffic is unpredictable or spiky — no capacity planning wanted

rows.label: Provisioned capacity
cells: Traffic is steady enough to plan RCU and WCU ahead, optionally with auto scaling

scenes.narration: A handful of real numbers the exam checks directly. Four hundred kilobytes is DynamoDB's hard maximum item size, completely unrelated to key design — anything bigger belongs in S3, with just a reference kept in the item. One read capacity unit — R C U — covers one strongly consistent read per second of up to four kilobytes; an eventually consistent read costs half that. One write capacity unit covers one write per second of up to one kilobyte. A Local Secondary Index shares the base table's ten gigabyte item-collection limit per partition key value, a separate ceiling from the four hundred kilobyte per-item limit. And DynamoDB Streams keep a rolling change log — commonly a twenty four hour window — that powers Global Tables replication and feeds Lambda for anything that needs to react to every write.

props.heading: Real limits, not vibes
bullets: Maximum item size: 400 KB, hard and real — bigger objects go in S3 with just a reference in the item.
One RCU: one strongly consistent read/sec of up to 4 KB — eventually consistent reads cost half that.
One write capacity unit: one write/sec of up to 1 KB.
LSIs share the base table's 10 GB item-collection limit per partition key value — separate from the 400 KB item limit.
DynamoDB Streams keep a rolling ~24-hour change log — the real mechanism behind Global Tables and Lambda triggers.

scenes.narration: First, create the base table with both keys defined up front: CustomerId as the partition key, using key type HASH, and OrderTs as the sort key, using key type RANGE — that exact vocabulary, HASH and RANGE, is what both the real A P I and the exam use. Next, add a Global Secondary Index to that same table after it's already live in production — this works precisely because a G S I isn't locked in at creation time the way an L S I is. Then query straight through that index with an index-name flag, a genuinely different access path than querying the base table. And finally, enable Time To Live — T T L — on an expiry attribute, so expired session data gets deleted automatically, in the background, without costing a single unit of write capacity.

props.heading: From create-table to a GSI query to automatic expiry

steps.cmd: aws dynamodb create-table --table-name Orders --attribute-definitions AttributeName=CustomerId,AttributeType=S AttributeName=OrderTs,AttributeType=S --key-schema AttributeName=CustomerId,KeyType=HASH AttributeName=OrderTs,KeyType=RANGE --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST

scenes.narration: Three files, three separate decisions. table.yaml locks in the partition key and sort key the moment the table is created — that one's permanent. gsi-order-status.yaml can be added independently, at any point in the table's life, because a Global Secondary Index was never tied to creation time in the first place. And dax-cluster.yaml is entirely optional, sitting in front of whichever reads turn out to be hot, without changing anything about how the table's keys were designed underneath it.

props.kicker: THE CLI, ORGANIZED BY WHEN IT CAN CHANGE
props.heading: orders-table/
lines: ├── table.yaml             # partition key + sort key — locked in at creation
└── dax-cluster.yaml       # optional, sits in front of hot reads

scenes.narration: Take a concrete case. A social app stores posts using CountryCode as the partition key, reasoning that grouping by country makes regional queries easy. After launch, more than half of all traffic turns out to come from users in a single country, and that one country's requests start throttling while the table's overall provisioned capacity is barely half used. The instinct to just raise the table's capacity doesn't touch the problem, because it's one overloaded physical partition, not an aggregate shortage. The real fix layers a better key underneath the same access pattern: a composite key combining CountryCode with a hash of the user ID, or partitioning by UserId directly and adding a G S I for the country lookup — spreading that one country's posts across many partitions instead of one.

props.heading: A social feed startup's CountryCode key

profile.name: A social feed startup
profile.role: Posts table partitioned by CountryCode · one country now over half of all traffic
profile.detail: CountryCode looked like a natural partition key because it made regional queries easy. After launch, that one country's requests throttle while the table's overall provisioned capacity is barely half used.
profile.verdict: Raising capacity doesn't fix a hot partition. The real fix: a composite key (CountryCode + a hash of UserId) or partition by UserId directly with a GSI for the country lookup — spreading that country's posts across many partitions instead of one.

scenes.narration: Try these before we reveal the answers. First: an application tries to store a six hundred kilobyte document as a single DynamoDB item — what actually happens, and why? Second, and this one's the professional-level version of the same underlying idea: a multi-tenant table partitioned by TenantId has one enterprise customer roughly two hundred times larger than a typical tenant, now seeing elevated latency and occasional throttling. What's really going on, and what's a fix that actually addresses it?

questions.prompt: An application tries to store a 600 KB document as a single DynamoDB item. What happens?
options: It succeeds — DynamoDB scales storage automatically regardless of item size.
It fails — 400 KB is DynamoDB's hard maximum item size, independent of capacity mode.
It succeeds, but only if the table is in on-demand capacity mode.
It fails only if the item also uses a composite sort key.

questions.prompt: A multi-tenant table partitioned by TenantId has one enterprise customer about 200 times larger than a typical tenant, now seeing elevated latency and occasional throttling. What's the real cause, and what fix actually addresses it?
options: A hidden account-wide request limit has been hit; open a support case to raise it.
That one tenant's data is concentrated on a small number of physical partitions regardless of table capacity — shard its key or move it to a dedicated table.
Nothing is wrong — DynamoDB always spreads load evenly no matter the key design.
Switching the table to strongly consistent reads will resolve the latency.

scenes.narration: Here's why. The four hundred kilobyte item limit is real, hard, and has nothing to do with capacity mode — the six hundred kilobyte document simply doesn't fit, and the correct pattern is storing it in S3 with a reference in the item instead. And the oversized tenant is a hot-partition problem in disguise: TenantId as the sole partition key concentrates that one tenant's entire dataset onto a small number of physical partitions no matter how many other tenants share the table, so sharding that tenant's key or giving it a dedicated table fixes the root cause — raising the shared table's overall provisioned capacity does not.

answers.prompt: Storing a 600 KB document as a single item.
answers.correct: It fails — 400 KB is the hard ceiling.
answers.rationale: DynamoDB's maximum item size is a real, stable 400 KB limit, unrelated to capacity mode or key design. Large documents belong in S3, with only a reference — like the object key — kept in the DynamoDB item itself.

answers.prompt: A tenant 200 times larger than average, on a table partitioned by TenantId.
answers.correct: It's a hot-partition problem tied to that tenant's size, not table capacity.
answers.rationale: TenantId as the sole partition key concentrates that one large tenant's entire dataset onto a small number of physical partitions, regardless of how many other tenants exist. Sharding that tenant's key, or moving it to a dedicated table, fixes the root cause; raising the shared table's overall provisioned capacity does not.

scenes.narration: Five things to carry forward. The partition key is a physical placement decision — DynamoDB hashes it to choose the partition, and that choice is what actually decides whether the table scales evenly. Four hundred kilobytes is the hard maximum item size, unrelated to capacity mode — big blobs belong in S3. A G S I can be added any time but is always eventually consistent; an L S I must be defined at table creation but can support strong consistency. A hot partition throttles a subset of requests even while aggregate capacity sits unused, and the fix is a better key, not more capacity — DAX only ever helps the read side. And on-demand suits unpredictable traffic while provisioned suits steady, planned traffic, as a deliberate choice rather than a dial to flip daily. Next: chapter ten moves up a layer into serverless compute, where Lambda's own hard fifteen-minute timeout, cold starts, and Step Functions orchestration read from and write to exactly the kind of DynamoDB tables this chapter just taught you to design well.

props.heading: What to remember from this chapter
takeaways: The partition key is a physical placement decision — DynamoDB hashes it to choose the partition, and that determines whether the table scales evenly.
400 KB is DynamoDB's hard maximum item size, unrelated to capacity mode — large blobs belong in S3 with just a reference in the item.
A GSI can be added any time but is always eventually consistent; an LSI must be defined at table creation but can support strong consistency.
A hot partition throttles a subset of requests even with capacity to spare — the fix is a better key, not more capacity, and DAX only helps reads.
On-demand suits unpredictable traffic, provisioned suits steady traffic — capacity mode is a deliberate choice, not a daily dial.

scenes.narration: One more to work through yourself. A game needs a live top one hundred leaderboard by score, updated constantly, plus each player's own personal stats page — and a per-player partition key can't answer "top N across everyone" efficiently at all. Using this chapter's framework, how would you design the keys and indexes to serve both access patterns? And why isn't a small, deliberately low-cardinality key automatically a design mistake here, even after everything this chapter just said about hot partitions?
